ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness Inspection | Houston, TX
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Houston refineries, chemical plants, tank farms and fab shops. Request a quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Houston, Texas
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs on-site ultrasonic testing in Houston: wall-thickness surveys on process piping, vessels and tanks, and shear-wave examination of welds in fabrication and repair work. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, yard or shop for the agreed scope, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. To scope a job, send the drawings or line list through our Houston UT quote request.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Houston

Houston is the center of US refining and petrochemical activity. The Houston area has ten refineries that together process about 2.6 million barrels of crude a day, and most of them sit along the Houston Ship Channel and Galveston Bay, surrounded by chemical plants, terminals and fabrication yards. That concentration creates a steady, repetitive need for thickness data. Crude and vacuum unit overhead lines, caustic and amine circuits, cooling-water piping, flare headers, fired heater outlets and the shells and heads of pressure vessels all lose wall over time, and the owner needs numbers to decide what stays in service through the next run.

The second large use is weld examination. Fabrication shops east and north of the city build pressure vessels, heat exchangers, pipe spools and offshore modules, and field crews make repair and tie-in welds during turnarounds. Where the construction code and the owner allow it, shear-wave UT examines those welds through their full thickness without the exposure zone that radiography requires. Tank farms along the channel add a third workload, with floor, shell and nozzle-neck readings on aboveground storage tanks and spheres.

What UT finds in Houston service, and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends sound into the steel and times the echoes. For a thickness job the instrument reports remaining wall between the probe and the back surface, which is why it is the standard tool for corrosion monitoring. Locally common damage includes general thinning under insulation, localized pitting in water-wetted lines, erosion at elbows and tees in high-velocity hydrocarbon service, and thinning at injection points.

The method has limits that matter on Gulf Coast equipment. Heavy scale, pitting and rough external surfaces scatter sound, so readings on poorly prepared metal can read thin, thick or not at all. Lamination in plate can mask the back wall. Coarse-grained cast and austenitic stainless welds attenuate shear waves, which makes weld examination there a matter for procedure qualification rather than assumption. UT also reports only what lies under the probe, so a sparse grid can miss a small pit between points. A good scope says how dense the grid is and why.

Codes and acceptance criteria behind Houston work

Acceptance always comes from the document that governs the equipment. For new construction and repair of pressure equipment that is usually ASME Section VIII Division 1, with Appendix 12 covering ultrasonic examination of welds, or ASME B31.3 for process piping, where paragraph 344.6 describes ultrasonic examination and Table 341.3.2 sets the criteria. ASME Section V Article 4 gives the weld examination method, Article 5 covers material examination, and Article 23 carries SE-797 for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement. Structural steel work is examined to AWS D1.1, which includes ultrasonic acceptance for groove welds.

For equipment already in service, the owner's inspection program draws on API 510 for vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for tanks. Under those programs the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection and for the remaining-life and interval decisions. Atlantis supplies the examination data: thickness at each condition monitoring location, indications found in welds, and the records that support the inspector's evaluation. The mechanical integrity element of OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), is why most facility owners in the area keep such records current.

Texas adds its own regime for boilers. The Texas Boiler Act, Chapter 755 of the Health and Safety Code, is administered by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, and covered boilers are inspected by commissioned inspectors. Intrastate pipelines fall under the Railroad Commission of Texas and interstate lines under PHMSA, with API 1104 incorporated for pipeline welding.

Technique: thickness readings and weld examination

A corrosion survey starts with a grid or a list of condition monitoring locations marked on an isometric or a vessel sketch, so that the same spot can be read again at the next inspection. The technician calibrates the instrument on a step block of the same material, using a dual-element probe for corroded or rough surfaces, and checks the calibration at set intervals during the job and again at the end. An A-scan display lets the technician see the waveform behind the number, which prevents the doubling errors that can appear on thin or pitted wall. On hot lines, high-temperature probes and couplant are used with temperature correction applied to the reading.

Weld examination uses angle-beam shear-wave probes, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees depending on thickness and joint geometry. The technician builds a reference level or distance-amplitude curve from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, scans the weld and heat-affected zone from both sides where access allows, and evaluates each reflector by amplitude, length and position. Lack of fusion, cracks and slag are the targets. Indications are reported against the code's acceptance table, not against personal judgment.

Turning readings into a corrosion rate

A single survey is a snapshot; the value comes from comparing it with the last one. When a Houston owner already holds baseline readings, technicians return to the same marked locations so that the difference in wall between two dates, divided by the time between them, gives a short-term corrosion rate. Dividing the margin above the minimum required thickness by that rate gives the owner a first view of remaining life, which the authorized inspector then confirms against the code. Consistency matters more than precision here: the same probe type, the same calibration approach and the same grid spacing keep scatter in the data from looking like corrosion. Where readings appear to rise between surveys, that usually points to a location error or a surface condition change, and the report should say so instead of quietly averaging it away.

Who does the work

Technicians who perform and interpret UT are qualified as Level II under the company written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. They set up and calibrate the equipment, carry out the examination and evaluate the results to the written procedure. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, approves the procedures and reviews reports. Atlantis does not operate a laboratory, yard or equipment depot in Houston, so all work is performed by technicians who travel to your site with calibrated instruments and the required blocks. Site orientation, badging and permit requirements are handled as part of mobilization planning.

What a Houston UT report contains

  • Component or line number, drawing reference and the location grid or condition monitoring location identifiers.
  • Procedure number and revision, the governing code and edition, and the acceptance table applied.
  • Instrument, probe, calibration block and couplant, with the calibration checks recorded through the job.
  • Technician name and certification level, plus the Level III reviewer.
  • For thickness work, a grid or table of readings with nominal and minimum required wall, and a note of any location that could not be read.
  • For weld work, each indication with position, length, amplitude and an accept or reject disposition, with sketches where useful.

Readings that fall below a threshold the owner has set are flagged in the report body, so the person who needs to act on them does not have to search a spreadsheet. Raw data stays available for trending against earlier surveys.

Surface preparation and couplant on Houston equipment

Ultrasound only enters steel through a continuous film of couplant, so the surface decides whether a reading is trustworthy. Gel or paste couplant suits most vertical and overhead locations in a plant, while hot lines need a high-temperature grade that does not boil off under the probe. Technicians clean each reading point of loose scale and flaking coating, and on pitted surfaces they may grind a small spot flat so the probe sits squarely. A reading taken over a pit bottom is different from a reading taken on sound metal beside it, and the report notes which was measured. Where coating remains tight and intact, a procedure can sometimes be demonstrated through it, but the Level III must approve that before the survey, not after.

Planning a UT job in Houston

Local conditions shape the schedule. Summer surface temperatures on uninsulated carbon steel can exceed what standard probes and couplant tolerate, so hot-surface technique has to be decided up front. Humid air and frequent rain interrupt outdoor weld examination on structures and pipe racks, and hurricane season can close a site for days. Plants along the ship channel usually require contractor safety orientation, gate badging and a permit for each work area, and turnaround weeks fill quickly with many crews on the same units, so the examination sequence should be agreed with the planner. Insulation removal and scaffold access for each location should be arranged before the technicians travel, because a technician waiting for scaffolding is a technician not taking readings. Fabrication shops are more predictable: parts are on the floor, lighting is controlled and the weld can be examined at the stage the code requires.

UT, MT or PT for your Houston job

Choose the method by the question. If the question is how much wall remains, or whether a weld is sound through its thickness, UT is the answer. If the question is whether a surface crack has formed at a toe or nozzle weld in carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Houston is quicker and more sensitive near the surface. For stainless, nickel alloy and aluminum, where magnetic methods do not work, liquid penetrant testing in Houston finds surface-breaking flaws. Many repair packages use two methods together: PT or MT on the surface and UT for the volume. The national ultrasonic testing page explains the method in general terms, and the Houston inspection services hub lists the other conventional examinations.

Training your own UT technicians

Many Houston employers prefer to build an in-house UT group. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with theory delivered online, simulator practice on the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator and hands-on practical work at the employer's facility. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer's written practice governs qualification, which the eligibility checker explains. See also NDT training in Houston.

faq.q: Do you perform ultrasonic thickness testing on hot piping in Houston?
faq.a: Yes, within the limits of the procedure. High-temperature probes and couplant are used with temperature correction, and the surface temperature, safe contact time and site permit rules are agreed with the plant before technicians mobilize to the unit.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on Houston pipe welds?
faq.a: Only where the construction code, the owner and the engineer allow it. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 have provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, and AWS D1.1 has its own groove-weld criteria. The substitution is agreed before work starts.

faq.q: What do I need to send for a UT thickness quote?
faq.a: Send line numbers or vessel tags, isometrics or sketches, material, nominal wall, operating temperature, insulation status and the number of locations. A prior survey helps, because new readings can be taken at the same condition monitoring locations.

faq.q: Who decides remaining life and inspection interval?
faq.a: The owner and its authorized inspector, under API 510, API 570 or API 653 as applicable. Atlantis performs the examination and delivers the thickness data and indications; it does not act as the inspector of record.

faq.q: Does insulation have to be removed for UT in Houston plants?
faq.a: For most direct-contact readings the metal surface must be exposed at each location, so the owner normally removes small insulation windows. Plugs and removable covers at condition monitoring locations make repeat surveys much simpler.

faq.q: What surface preparation does UT need?
faq.a: The surface must be free of loose scale, flaking paint, weld spatter and heavy rust so the probe can couple. Light wire brushing or grinding is often enough for thickness work; weld examination needs scanning surfaces cleared on both sides of the weld.

faq.q: Do you work in Houston fabrication shops as well as plants?
faq.a: Yes. Weld examination at the shop stage, before painting or insulation, is often the simplest time to examine, and technicians can travel to the shop to examine welds to the code and customer specification.

faq.q: How is UT qualified under SNT-TC-1A?
faq.a: The employer writes a practice based on SNT-TC-1A that sets training hours, experience, examinations and records for each level. Level II technicians perform the work, and a Level III approves procedures and reviews reports.

faq.q: How is the grid spacing for a thickness survey chosen?
faq.a: It follows the damage mechanism and the owner program. Uniform thinning allows a wider spacing, while localized pitting, erosion at elbows or injection points calls for a tighter grid. The spacing is stated in the scope and the report so later surveys can match it.

faq.q: Can my team learn UT instead of hiring it?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training with online theory, simulator practice and hands-on work at your facility, and can help write the written practice that governs qualification.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Houston, TX | MT
mt.description: Mag particle testing for Houston refinery vessels, pipe racks, crane lifts and fab-shop welds, wet fluorescent or visible dry, yoke or prods. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Houston, Texas
mt.html:
Magnetic particle inspection finds cracks that open to the surface, or lie just beneath it, in carbon and low-alloy steel. Atlantis NDT sends qualified technicians to Houston refineries, chemical plants, fabrication yards and lifting-equipment sites to examine welds, nozzles, attachments, castings and forgings. Procedures are written to the governing code and approved by an ASNT NDT Level III. Describe the parts and the applicable code in a Houston MT quote request.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Houston

Steel is the dominant material in the Houston industrial belt, which makes MT a daily tool. Refinery and chemical equipment in the ship channel corridor is full of attachment welds, nozzle-to-shell welds, support lugs, skirt-to-shell junctions and repair weld buildup, and each of those is a place where a toe crack can start. During a vessel entry, technicians examine internal weld seams after cleaning; on the outside, they examine nozzle and saddle welds and pipe-support attachments on racks that run for miles through the plants.

Fabrication shops produce more MT work than most visitors expect. Pressure vessel, skid and offshore module builders examine structural joints, lifting lugs and heavy-wall welds before coating. Heavy lifting also drives demand: cranes, pad eyes, shackles, hooks and spreader beams used on yards and docks need periodic surface examination because fatigue cracks start at the surface and grow under cyclic loads. Drilling-equipment repair shops across the metro area use MT on threaded connections and load-bearing forgings as well.

What MT finds, and what it cannot

The method magnetizes the part, so a discontinuity that cuts across the field leaks flux, and fine ferromagnetic particles gather over the leak and form a visible indication. That sets clear boundaries. MT works only on ferromagnetic material: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic grades respond, while austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and most nickel alloys do not, so those need a different method. It detects surface and slightly subsurface discontinuities and says nothing reliable about flaws deeper in the wall.

Orientation matters. A crack parallel to the magnetic field produces almost no leakage, which is why the examination is made twice with the field direction changed by roughly ninety degrees. Thick paint or coating, rough surfaces, weld spatter and oil reduce sensitivity, and very sharp geometry can create nonrelevant particle buildup that a trained examiner must separate from real cracking. In wet hydrogen sulfide service, surface-breaking cracking at weld toes is a recognized concern, which is one reason refinery owners specify MT at those welds after repairs.

Codes and acceptance for Houston MT work

Methods and acceptance come from the equipment's construction or maintenance code. ASME Section V Article 7 sets the examination method. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 gives MT methods and acceptance standards for pressure vessels, and ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with Table 341.3.2 governs process piping. Structural work follows AWS D1.1, bridge steel follows AWS D1.5, and ASTM E709 and E1444 describe the practice and guide. Lifting equipment often follows the manufacturer's or owner's specification instead of a construction code, which the procedure must name.

Texas boiler work falls under the Texas Boiler Act, Chapter 755 of the Health and Safety Code, administered by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation. For vessels and piping in refineries, the owner's inspection program under API 510 and API 570 and its OSHA process safety management obligations in 29 CFR 1910.119(j) set the expectations, and the owner's authorized inspector makes the fitness decision. Atlantis performs the examination and reports the indications; it does not act as the inspector of record.

Technique: yokes, prods, particles and demagnetization

Most field work in Houston uses an electromagnetic yoke. An AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, a check the technician performs with a test weight. The yoke is placed across the weld in two positions roughly at right angles so cracks in any direction are caught. Prods, where permitted by the procedure, drive current through the part, but burn marks on finished surfaces make many owners ban them on pressure-retaining items.

Visible dry powder suits hot or rough surfaces outdoors, while visible wet particles in aerosol cans are common on cleaner weld surfaces, usually over a thin white contrast paint. Fluorescent wet particles give the highest sensitivity but need UV-A light and a darkened area, with intensity and ambient white-light limits set by the code. After the examination the surface is cleaned, and parts are demagnetized when a residual field would interfere with welding, machining or later operations. Technicians record the yoke checks, the particle batch and the field direction used.

Surface condition and preparation

Sensitivity begins with the surface. Particles must be able to move and cluster over a leakage field, so oil, grease, loose scale, slag and heavy paint all work against the examination. On new fabrication the weld is normally ground or brushed to clean metal and the adjacent base metal is cleaned a short distance on each side. On in-service equipment, a refinery owner often removes coating from small windows at weld locations, and a wire brush or flap disc handles heavy rust. Where contrast paint is applied for visible wet particles, it must be thin and dry before the particles go on, since a thick film weakens the field at the surface. Preparation is agreed in advance so the technician arrives to a surface that is ready, and the report records any area that could not be prepared.

Common indications and how they are judged

A crack usually shows as a sharp, tight line of particles, often along the weld toe or in the heat-affected zone. Lack of fusion at the surface shows as a straighter line along the fusion boundary. Porosity and slag that reach the surface show as rounded or irregular groups. Not every cluster is a defect: sharp changes in section, magnetic writing from contact with other steel and the edge of a weld can hold particles without being a flaw. The examiner separates relevant from nonrelevant indications by re-examining, cleaning, remagnetizing and, if necessary, changing the field direction. Only relevant indications are compared with the acceptance table, and the same table sets the maximum length and number allowed. A rejected crack is normally marked, removed by grinding, and the area is re-examined to confirm that the flaw is gone before welding resumes.

Who performs and reviews the work

Level II technicians qualified under the company's SNT-TC-1A-based written practice perform and interpret the examination. An ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports; the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis keeps no depot, laboratory or yard in Houston, so technicians travel to your site with their own yokes, particles and light meters and are mobilized for the agreed scope only. Calibration of the yokes and meters is current and recorded before the job.

What the MT report shows

  • Part, tag or weld identification and the area examined, with a sketch for complex geometry.
  • Procedure and revision, the code and edition, and the acceptance criteria used.
  • Yoke or equipment type, lift test results, particle type and color, contrast paint and light readings.
  • Surface temperature and condition at the time of the examination.
  • Each indication with location, length and orientation, whether it is relevant, and the accept or reject call.
  • Technician name and level, Level III reviewer and date.

Rejected indications can be photographed with a scale and marked on the part for the repair crew, and the re-examination after grinding is recorded in the same report.

Lifting equipment, forgings and castings

Not every MT job in Houston involves a weld. Heavy rigging used in yards and on docks, such as hooks, shackles, spreader beams, pad eyes and padeye attachments, is examined periodically because fatigue cracks start at the surface in highly stressed corners. Drilling-equipment repair shops across the metro area examine threaded connections and load-bearing forgings, and foundries and machine shops check castings after heat treatment and machining. For these parts there is often no construction code: the manufacturer's specification, the owner's program or a customer standard supplies the acceptance criteria, and the Level III writes the procedure around it. Where a part is magnetized with a coil or a head-and-tail bench unit in a shop, field direction is controlled by the geometry, and a field indicator confirms the field is adequate before particles are applied.

Planning an MT job in Houston

Heat and humidity drive the planning. Dry powder works on warm steel, but wet particle carriers and contrast paint need the surface within the temperature range the procedure allows, and a sun-baked pipe rack may be too hot to examine at midday. Humid air and frequent rain can wash particles off or stop outdoor work altogether, so tents and scheduling flexibility help. Fluorescent work demands darkness, which usually means a dark enclosure or night shift, and that has to be approved with the plant. Many facilities along the channel require site orientation, hot-work or confined-space permits and escorts, so technicians cannot simply walk onto the unit. Surface preparation is the owner's usual responsibility: paint, scale and slag should be removed back to clean metal before the examination day. Turnaround periods are crowded, so ask for the sequence early and keep the examination close to the final weld pass so repairs do not stall the schedule.

MT, PT or UT for your Houston job

If the part is carbon steel and the question is surface cracking, MT is usually quicker and more sensitive than penetrant. If the material is stainless, aluminum or nickel alloy, use dye penetrant inspection in Houston instead. If the concern lies below the surface or concerns remaining wall, ultrasonic testing in Houston is the right tool. The national magnetic particle testing page and the ASME Section V guide to Article 7 requirements explain the method further, and the MT versus PT comparison helps when materials are mixed.

Training your own MT technicians

Houston employers with steady weld repair work often train their own examiners. MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training start with online theory, followed by practical work at the employer's facility under the written practice. For wider options see NDT training in Houston and, for companies that need a written practice, written practice development.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel pipe in Houston plants?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel is not ferromagnetic, so particles will not form indications. Use liquid penetrant on stainless and nickel alloy piping. Duplex and martensitic grades can behave differently, so confirm with the procedure.

faq.q: What is the difference between wet fluorescent and visible dry MT?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent particles under UV-A light give the highest sensitivity and need a dark area. Visible dry powder is simpler on hot or rough surfaces outdoors but is less sensitive to very fine cracks.

faq.q: Do you use prods on Houston pressure vessels?
faq.a: Usually not. Prods can leave arc burns on pressure-retaining surfaces, so many owners prohibit them. A yoke is the normal choice, and the procedure states what is allowed.

faq.q: Does MT detect cracks below the weld surface?
faq.a: Only slightly subsurface ones, and with reduced sensitivity as depth grows. For flaws deeper in the weld, use ultrasonic examination or another volumetric method agreed with the owner.

faq.q: Is demagnetizing always required after MT?
faq.a: No. It is required when residual magnetism would interfere with later welding, machining, instrument operation or service. The procedure or specification states when, and the report records that it was done.

faq.q: Can paint stay on during magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Thin, tight coatings may be allowed if the procedure has been demonstrated through them, but thick or flaking paint reduces sensitivity. Most Houston specifications call for bare metal at welds.

faq.q: Can you examine crane hooks and lifting lugs?
faq.a: Yes. Surface cracks at load-bearing points are a classic MT target. The owner or manufacturer specification supplies the acceptance criteria, and the procedure names it before work starts.

faq.q: How do you confirm the magnetic field is strong enough?
faq.a: Technicians use a yoke lift test and a field indicator or gauss meter, as the procedure requires, and record the result. The ASME Section V rules also require two examinations with the field direction changed.

faq.q: What do I send to get an MT quote?
faq.a: Send the equipment type, material, number and size of welds or parts, surface condition, location, applicable code or specification, and the timing of any turnaround or shutdown that sets the schedule.

faq.q: Who is responsible for deciding if an indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The examination report applies the named acceptance criteria. Where fitness-for-service or repair decisions follow, the owner and its authorized inspector decide. Atlantis reports the data and the code evaluation.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Houston, TX | Liquid PT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing for Houston stainless piping, alloy overlays, castings and machined parts. Visible and fluorescent PT on site. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Houston, Texas
pt.html:
Liquid penetrant testing reveals cracks, laps and porosity that are open to the surface of non-porous material, whether it is magnetic or not. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to Houston plants, shops and yards to examine stainless and alloy piping welds, overlay and cladding, castings, forgings and machined components with visible or fluorescent penetrant. An ASNT NDT Level III approves each procedure. Send the material list and code in a Houston PT quote request.

Where penetrant testing is used in Houston

Houston's chemical and refining complexes use far more than carbon steel, and penetrant is the surface method for the rest. Stainless and duplex piping in chemical units, nickel alloy lines in high-temperature service, corrosion-resistant weld overlay on vessel internals and tube-to-tubesheet welds on heat exchangers all need a method that does not depend on magnetism. Pump casings, valve bodies, compressor components and impellers pass through repair shops across the metro area, where penetrant checks castings and machined surfaces before and after rework.

Fabrication yards building vessels and modules use PT on root passes of stainless pipe, on weld buildup and on repaired areas of cast fittings. Offshore and marine support yards along the channel examine aluminum and stainless components from deck equipment and heat-exchange packages. The same method also double-checks carbon steel welds where an owner specifies penetrant instead of magnetic particle, for example on a coated or contoured area where a yoke will not seat well.

What PT finds, and what it cannot

Penetrant liquid seeps into surface-breaking flaws, a developer draws it back out, and the stain makes the flaw visible. The method is therefore limited to discontinuities that are open to the surface. A crack closed by peening, grinding smear, heavy oxide or a previous cleaning step can hide completely, and subsurface flaws never appear at all. Porous materials absorb penetrant and produce a general background, so PT does not suit them.

The strengths are broad: it works on nearly any non-porous metal, ceramic or plastic, requires no power on site and shows the length and shape of a crack plainly. Its weaknesses are cleanliness and temperature. Oil, paint, rust and chemical residue block entry, and a surface outside the procedure's temperature window changes penetrant behavior. Hydrogen-service and high-strength equipment sometimes call for a higher-sensitivity fluorescent system, while austenitic materials call for penetrant products low in halogens and sulfur, because residues can attack the metal in service.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Houston PT work

The method itself is described in ASME Section V Article 6. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 gives PT methods and acceptance for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 cover process piping, and ASTM E165 is the common practice standard for general industry. Structural stainless work may follow AWS D1.6, and repair of boilers and pressure vessels is governed by the National Board Inspection Code with the Texas Boiler Act, Chapter 755 of the Health and Safety Code, applying to boilers in Texas.

In-service equipment is generally inspected under the owner's API 510 and API 570 programs, with mechanical integrity duties under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j). The owner's authorized inspector accepts the findings; Atlantis performs the examination and documents each indication. Material-specific restrictions, such as limits on chlorides and sulfur in penetrant materials for stainless and nickel alloys, are written into the procedure and checked on the product batch certificates.

Technique: from precleaning to final evaluation

The result depends on preparation. The technician cleans the area by grinding, brushing and solvent so the surface is free of oil, scale, paint and weld spatter, then dries it. The standard range for the part and the penetrant materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit; outside that range the procedure must be qualified for the temperature, which matters on a cold winter morning or a sun-heated rack in a Houston summer.

Penetrant is applied by spray or brush and left to dwell for the time the procedure states, usually several minutes depending on material and flaw type. Excess is removed by solvent wipe, water wash or post-emulsification, depending on the system. Developer, typically a thin white non-aqueous film, is sprayed on and given development time before the technician examines the surface under white light or, for fluorescent systems, UV-A light in a darkened area. Indications are evaluated by size and shape against the acceptance criteria, then the surface is cleaned again. Technicians record the penetrant system, batch numbers, dwell and development times and temperature.

Precleaning pitfalls on Houston equipment

Most failed penetrant examinations fail before any penetrant goes on. Equipment in process service carries hydrocarbon films, amine, caustic and polymer residues that can fill a crack and keep penetrant out, and shot-blasted or wire-brushed surfaces can smear metal over fine openings. A sound sequence is mechanical removal of scale and coating, solvent or detergent cleaning, a drying period long enough for solvent to leave the flaw, and a check that the surface is dry. On weld overlays and cladding, grinding followed by a light etch can reopen smeared metal when the procedure allows it. Cleaning solvents must also suit the alloy, because chloride-bearing products are unacceptable on austenitic stainless, so the owner's materials rules are read before the kit is packed.

Common indications and how they are judged

Cracks appear as continuous or intermittent red or fluorescent lines, porosity as rounded dots, and laps or cold shuts as irregular lines on the surface. Bleedout that spreads quickly suggests a large opening, while a slow, faint bleed suggests a tight crack, so the time of appearance is itself evidence. Nonrelevant indications come from rough surfaces, weld ripples, residual penetrant on a thread or a poorly removed excess, and the examiner re-cleans and re-tests the area to confirm. Relevant indications are measured and compared with the acceptance table: linear indications are usually evaluated by length, and rounded ones by size and spacing. The result is recorded as accepted or rejected, and rejected defects are marked, removed or repaired and re-examined.

High-sensitivity systems for critical service

Some Houston equipment is in service where a very small crack can matter: hydrogen-bearing units, rotating equipment and highly stressed forgings are examples. Owners often specify a fluorescent system at a higher sensitivity level for those items, together with a longer dwell and a controlled development time. The trade-off is that background fluorescence from rough or poorly washed surfaces rises with sensitivity, so more cleaning care is needed and the area must be darkened. Where a procedure names a particular sensitivity level, the batch and level are written in the report so a later reviewer can see exactly what system was used.

Who performs the work

PT is carried out by Level II technicians qualified under the company's SNT-TC-1A-based written practice. Level III oversight comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, who approves procedures and reviews reports. Because Atlantis has no laboratory, depot or yard in Houston, technicians travel to your facility with a kit of cleaners, penetrant, developer, lights and comparator blocks, and the materials are matched to the alloy under test and to the owner's contaminant limits.

What a PT report includes

  • Part, spool or weld identification, material and the area examined.
  • Procedure and revision, the code and acceptance table, and the penetrant system and sensitivity level.
  • Product manufacturer and batch numbers, with contaminant certificate reference for stainless and nickel alloys.
  • Surface temperature, dwell time and development time.
  • Each indication by location, dimensions and type, relevant or nonrelevant, with the accept or reject call.
  • Technician, certification level, Level III reviewer and date, plus photographs where useful.

A rejected area is marked for repair, and the re-examination after repair is covered in the same record so the weld history stays in one place.

Shop and field setups compared

A penetrant examination in a fabrication shop can use a stationary line with controlled lighting, but most Houston plant work is done in the field with aerosol cans and wipe-off cleaning. The field method trades some repeatability for access: wind, dust and sun affect dwell, and a technician working from a ladder cannot easily control the amount of developer applied. Experienced examiners compensate by shading the work, applying developer in thin even coats and timing each step. Where a specification requires water-washable penetrant on rough castings, the shop line is the better choice, and parts can be sent to a suitable facility selected by the owner. The procedure states which setup applies so that results from shop and field remain comparable.

Planning a PT job in Houston

Weather and facility rules decide most of the schedule. Midday heat can push exposed steel above the procedure's upper limit, and penetrant can dry before it has dwelled, so work is often done early or in shade. Winter mornings occasionally drop below the lower limit, which calls for warming the part or a qualified low-temperature procedure. Rain and high humidity slow drying and development. Penetrant materials are flammable and chemical, so plants require safety data sheets and may restrict aerosols, solvents or sparks near operating units, and confined-space entry needs permits and standby personnel. On stainless and alloy equipment, tell us early which materials and contaminant limits apply, because the penetrant products have to be selected and documented before the job. Insist on surface preparation by the owner or the fabricator, since a poorly prepared weld wastes the visit.

PT, MT or UT for your Houston job

Use PT when the material is non-magnetic or the geometry does not suit a yoke. For carbon steel where speed and sensitivity matter, magnetic particle testing in Houston may be quicker. If the question is wall loss or buried flaws, UT inspection in Houston answers it. The general penetrant testing page, the Article 6 explainer and the MT versus PT guide give more detail.

Training your own PT technicians

Penetrant is the quickest method for new technicians to learn, which suits shops that want in-house capability. PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training combine online theory with practice on the penetrant testing simulator and hands-on sessions at the employer's site. See NDT training in Houston for every method.

faq.q: Which material can be examined with liquid penetrant?
faq.a: Any clean, non-porous material works, including stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium and carbon steel. Porous materials absorb the liquid and cause a general background that hides real indications.

faq.q: Why does penetrant temperature matter in Houston?
faq.a: The standard temperature range for the part and penetrant is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside it the procedure must be qualified for the temperature, and Houston summer sun can heat exposed steel past that limit.

faq.q: Can PT find a crack that has been ground or peened over?
faq.a: Often not. Smeared metal can close the opening so the penetrant cannot enter. Etching or careful preparation helps, and the procedure may require it where machining or grinding preceded the examination.

faq.q: What penetrant is used on stainless steel pipe?
faq.a: Products with controlled halogen and sulfur content are used on austenitic stainless and nickel alloys, with batch certificates on file. The procedure names the approved materials and the cleaning steps afterward.

faq.q: Is fluorescent penetrant better than visible penetrant?
faq.a: Fluorescent systems are more sensitive and favored for critical or fatigue-prone parts, but need UV-A light and a dark area. Visible systems are easier in the field and suitable for many weld examinations.

faq.q: Does PT detect subsurface flaws?
faq.a: No. Only discontinuities open to the surface can draw penetrant into them. Buried lack of fusion or inclusions need ultrasonic examination or another volumetric method agreed with the owner.

faq.q: Do you perform PT on shop-fabricated spools?
faq.a: Yes. Examination at the weld stage, before coating or insulation, is straightforward, and technicians can travel to the shop to examine root passes, buildup and finished welds to the specification.

faq.q: What cleanup follows a penetrant examination?
faq.a: Residual developer and penetrant are removed after evaluation, especially on parts that will be welded, coated or placed in oxygen or chemical service. The procedure sets the cleaning method and the report records it.

faq.q: Can PT be used on a weld that is still hot?
faq.a: Only within the procedure temperature limits. Hot welds can evaporate penetrant before it dwells, so the weld is cooled into the qualified range first or a procedure qualified for the higher temperature is used.

faq.q: What details are needed for a PT quote?
faq.a: Send materials, component types, number of welds or parts, surface finish, temperature conditions, applicable code and any restrictions on chemicals, along with the schedule or outage that sets the timing.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in Houston, TX: UT Alternative & Review
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For Houston welds we offer ultrasonic examination where code allows, plus Level III review of radiographs.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing in Houston, Texas: What Atlantis Does and Does Not Offer
rt.html:
Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. Industrial radiography uses sealed gamma sources or X-ray equipment and is a licensed activity, regulated by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission under 10 CFR Part 34 or by the equivalent rules of an Agreement State such as Texas. It is not a service we sell in Houston or anywhere else in the country. If you searched for radiography here, the sections below explain what we do offer for the same weld-quality questions.

Ultrasonic examination as the volumetric alternative in Houston

For many welds in Houston plants and fabrication shops, shear-wave ultrasonic examination answers the question a film would answer: is there lack of fusion, a crack or slag inside the weld? Our technicians are mobilized to your site for this work. Whether ultrasonic examination may stand in for radiography depends on the document that governs the weld. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII allows ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under specific conditions. The owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector must agree to the substitution before the job begins. Details of the method are on the Houston ultrasonic testing page, and you can request a scope through the Houston quote form.

Level III review of radiographs, with no radiation licence needed

Reading an image carries no radiation hazard, so an ASNT Level III can review work that another party has produced, which makes it a useful service for owners who must defend an acceptance decision to an auditor. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, can check film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. Typical requests from Houston owners and contractors include:

  • A second read on disputed or borderline indications before a weld is cut out.
  • Review of image quality, penetrameter or wire sensitivity, density and coverage on a completed package.
  • Review of a radiography contractor's written procedure and technique sheets against the code.
  • Review of the contractor's written practice and the qualification records behind it.

We review submitted records only. We do not recommend or name a radiography contractor, and exposure planning stays with the licensed provider and your site safety group.

If your project specification requires radiography, the licensed provider you select will normally issue film or images with a technique sheet, and the review described above can be arranged separately from that contract.

Surface methods that complement the volumetric examination

Many Houston repair packages combine a volumetric method with surface examination. Magnetic particle inspection in Houston covers carbon and low-alloy steel, and liquid penetrant testing in Houston covers stainless steel, nickel alloys and aluminum. Both are performed to ASME Section V procedures approved by a Level III. The Houston inspection services hub lists the full set of conventional examinations available.

Radiographic testing training and written practice support

Studying radiography theory carries no licence requirement, though handling sources does. Our RT Level 2 course covers the principles, image interpretation and code criteria, and the hands-on and source-handling portions belong to the licensed employer. Companies that qualify their own personnel can use our Level III consulting and written practice development to build a program around ASNT SNT-TC-1A. For a general explanation of weld examination options, the Houston NDT training page lists the programs available.

faq.q: Is radiography available from Atlantis in Houston?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography requires a radioactive materials or X-ray licence under NRC rules or Texas rules. We offer ultrasonic examination and Level III review instead.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my Houston piping welds?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 have provisions for ultrasonic examination, and AWS D1.1 has criteria for groove welds. The owner, engineer and authorized inspector must agree to the substitution before work starts.

faq.q: Can you review radiographs produced by another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. A Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, which gives a documented second opinion without any radiation work.

faq.q: Do you recommend a radiography contractor in Houston?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. Choose a licensed provider through your own approved vendor process, and we can review the procedure and the results if you ask.

faq.q: Can my staff learn radiographic theory with Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. The RT Level 2 course covers theory and interpretation. Source handling and exposure work require a radioactive materials or X-ray licence held by the employer, so those parts are outside our scope.
